title: Matter and the Changes It Undergoes
subject: Science
chapter: Matter and the changes it undergoes
description: Comprehensive practice for the whole book: what matter is; solids, liquids and gases; changes of state; heat; reversible vs irreversible changes; solutions; soluble/insoluble; miscible/immiscible; and methods of separation.

questions.question: What is matter?
options: Anything that has mass and takes up space
questions.explanation: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space — a rock, water and even air are all matter.

questions.question: Air is matter because it has mass and takes up space.
questions.explanation: Even though we cannot see it, air has mass and fills space, so it is matter.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT matter?
questions.explanation: A shadow has no mass and takes up no space, so it is not matter. Rocks, water and air are all matter.

questions.question: Select ALL the examples of matter.
questions.explanation: Rock, water and air all have mass and take up space. Sunlight is a form of energy, not matter.

questions.question: The thirsty crow raised the water by dropping in stones. What does this show?
options: Two forms of matter cannot occupy the same space
questions.explanation: The stones and water are both matter, and two things cannot share the same space — so the water level rises as stones fill the pitcher.

questions.question: Two pieces of matter can share the exact same space at the same time.
questions.explanation: Two forms of matter cannot occupy the same space — that is why dropping stones into a pitcher pushes the water up.

questions.question: How many main states of matter are there?
questions.explanation: The three main states of matter are solids, liquids and gases.

questions.question: Which of these are the three main states of matter? (Select all)
questions.explanation: Solid, liquid and gas are the three states of matter. 'Powder' is just a solid broken into tiny bits.

questions.question: Which state of matter has BOTH a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
questions.explanation: Solids keep the same shape and the same volume, like a pencil or a desk.

questions.question: Which of these is a solid?
questions.explanation: A pencil has a fixed shape and volume, so it is a solid. Water is liquid; air and steam are gases.

questions.question: A pencil keeps the same shape whether it is on your desk or in your bag.
questions.explanation: Solids keep a fixed shape no matter where they are placed.

questions.question: A liquid takes the shape of its ____ but keeps the same volume.
questions.explanation: A liquid flows to fit its container's shape, but the amount (volume) stays the same.

questions.question: A liquid changes its volume when poured into a differently shaped container.
questions.explanation: A liquid changes its shape to fit the container, but its volume stays the same.

questions.question: Juice looks rectangular in a box and round in a bottle. What stays the same?
questions.explanation: The shape changes to match the container, but the amount of juice (its volume) does not change.

questions.question: Which state of matter has NO fixed shape and NO fixed volume?
questions.explanation: Gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume — they spread out to fill their container.

questions.question: Which statement about gases is correct?
options: Gases have no fixed shape or volume and can expand or compress
questions.explanation: Gases can expand to fill a big space or be compressed into a small one; they have no fixed shape or volume.

questions.question: Gases have a fixed volume, just like liquids.
questions.explanation: Liquids have a fixed volume, but gases do NOT — they expand or compress to fill their container.

questions.question: Why can you smell incense from the far side of a room?
options: A gas spreads out to fill the space
questions.explanation: A gas spreads to fill any space, so the fragrance reaches every corner of the room.

questions.question: Air inside a balloon expands when it is ____.
questions.explanation: Heating a gas makes it expand, so the air in a balloon takes up more space when warmed.

questions.question: You can feel the air from a fan even though you cannot see it.
questions.explanation: Air is a gas — you can feel it but not see it.

questions.question: Select ALL the gases.
questions.explanation: Air, water vapour and steam are gases. Milk is a liquid.

questions.question: Which of these is a liquid?
questions.explanation: Milk flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid.

questions.question: Select ALL the solids.
questions.explanation: A rock and a pencil have a fixed shape and volume. Water is a liquid and air is a gas.

questions.question: Ink in a pen is a liquid because it takes the shape of the pen.
questions.explanation: Ink flows and fits the shape of its container, so it is a liquid.

questions.question: A desk stays the same shape and size whether you sit at it or move it. A desk is a ____.
questions.explanation: A desk keeps a fixed shape and volume, so it is a solid.

questions.question: Which list is ordered from MOST fixed shape to LEAST fixed shape?
questions.explanation: Solids have a fixed shape, liquids take the container's shape, and gases have no fixed shape at all.

questions.question: Which state of matter can be compressed (squeezed into a smaller space)?
questions.explanation: Gases can be compressed — that is how compressed air is squeezed into a tire.

questions.question: Solids can flow and take the shape of their container.
questions.explanation: Solids keep a fixed shape. Liquids and gases are the ones that flow to fit their container.

questions.question: Liquids can flow and be poured easily.
questions.explanation: Liquids flow, which is why they can be poured from one container to another.

questions.question: The word 'liquid' comes from the Latin word 'liquidus', which means ____.
questions.explanation: 'Liquidus' is Latin for 'flowing' — liquids flow and pour easily.

questions.question: The word 'gas' comes from which Greek word?
questions.explanation: 'Gas' comes from the Greek word 'chaos', because gases fill spaces invisibly and move about freely.

questions.question: Glass is made from melted ____.
questions.explanation: Glass is made by melting sand — so a window is really transformed sand.

questions.question: Every time you look through a window, you are seeing transformed sand.
questions.explanation: Glass is made from melted sand, so a glass window comes from sand.

questions.question: At petrol stations, compressed air is used to ____.
questions.explanation: Compressed air fills tires and keeps the right tire pressure for safe driving.

questions.question: Ice melting into water is a change from ____.
questions.explanation: Melting changes a solid (ice) into a liquid (water).

questions.question: What is the change from a liquid to a gas called?
questions.explanation: When a liquid turns into a gas it is called evaporation (Liquid → Gas).

questions.question: What is the change from a gas to a liquid called?
questions.explanation: When a gas cools into a liquid it is called condensation (Gas → Liquid).

questions.question: What is the change from a liquid to a solid called?
questions.explanation: When a liquid cools into a solid it is called freezing (Liquid → Solid).

questions.question: What is the change from a solid to a liquid called?
questions.explanation: When a solid warms into a liquid it is called melting (Solid → Liquid).

questions.question: Water droplets forming on the outside of a cold glass is an example of ____.
questions.explanation: Water vapour in the air cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid droplets — that is condensation.

questions.question: The water vapour turns into droplets on a cold glass because it ____.
questions.explanation: Cooling the water vapour makes it condense from a gas into liquid droplets.

questions.question: Wet clothes dry because the water in them evaporates into the air.
questions.explanation: Evaporation turns the liquid water in the clothes into water vapour, so the clothes dry.

questions.question: What is the key difference between evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation only happens indoors, boiling only outdoors
Evaporation needs very high heat, boiling happens at room temperature
They are exactly the same process
Evaporation is slow and at the surface, while boiling is fast and happens throughout the liquid
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a slow change at the surface of a liquid; boiling is fast and happens all through the liquid.

questions.question: Boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, not only at the surface.
questions.explanation: Boiling is fast and bubbly and happens all through the liquid, unlike slow surface-level evaporation.

questions.question: Butter melting in a hot pan is an example of ____.
questions.explanation: Heat melts the solid butter into a liquid (Solid → Liquid).

questions.question: Ice cubes melting in lemonade turn from ____.
questions.explanation: The ice (solid) gains heat energy and melts into water (liquid).

questions.question: Water placed in a freezer becomes ice. This change is called ____.
questions.explanation: Cooling liquid water until it becomes solid ice is freezing.

questions.question: What is sublimation?
options: A solid turning directly into a gas
A liquid turning into a gas
A gas turning into a liquid
A solid turning into a liquid
questions.explanation: Sublimation is when a solid changes straight into a gas without becoming a liquid first.

questions.question: Dry ice turning into gas without becoming liquid first is an example of ____.
questions.explanation: Dry ice sublimates — it goes straight from solid to gas.

questions.question: What is deposition?
options: A gas turning directly into a solid
A solid turning into a gas
A liquid turning into a solid
A gas turning into a liquid
questions.explanation: Deposition is the reverse of sublimation — a gas turns straight into a solid.

questions.question: Frost forming on a cold window is an example of ____.
questions.explanation: Water vapour (gas) turns straight into solid frost — that is deposition.

questions.question: Clouds form when water vapour ____ in the sky.
questions.explanation: Water vapour condenses into tiny droplets that gather to form clouds.

questions.question: Every cloud is made of tiny water droplets.
questions.explanation: Clouds are made of tiny droplets formed when water vapour condenses.

questions.question: Select ALL the changes that produce a LIQUID.
questions.explanation: Condensation (gas→liquid) and melting (solid→liquid) both make a liquid. Freezing makes a solid and evaporation makes a gas.

questions.question: When steam cools down and turns back into water, this is called ____.
questions.explanation: Steam (gas) cooling into water (liquid) is condensation.

questions.question: Which change of state is correctly matched: Liquid → Gas?
questions.explanation: Evaporation changes a liquid into a gas.

questions.question: Which change of state is correctly matched: Gas → Liquid?
questions.explanation: Condensation changes a gas into a liquid.

questions.question: Which change of state is correctly matched: Liquid → Solid?
questions.explanation: Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.

questions.question: Ice cream melting on a hot day is a change of ____.
questions.explanation: Melting ice cream is a change of state — solid to liquid.

questions.question: Water boiling in a kettle is rapid and bubbly.
questions.explanation: Boiling is a fast, bubbly change that happens throughout the water.

questions.question: Evaporation happens at the ____ of a liquid.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a slow change that happens at the surface of a liquid.

questions.question: Melting and boiling are the same change of state.
questions.explanation: Melting turns a solid into a liquid, while boiling turns a liquid into a gas — they are different.

questions.question: Deposition is the reverse of sublimation.
questions.explanation: Sublimation is solid→gas; deposition is gas→solid — they are opposites.

questions.question: Adding heat to ice causes it to ____.
questions.explanation: Heat gives energy to the ice particles, melting it into water.

questions.question: Removing heat from steam causes it to ____.
questions.explanation: Cooling steam removes energy, so it condenses into liquid water droplets.

questions.question: All changes of state involve gaining or losing ____ energy.
questions.explanation: Changes of state happen when heat energy is added or removed.

questions.question: Melting happens when a substance is heated; freezing happens when it is ____.
questions.explanation: Removing heat (cooling) turns a liquid into a solid — that is freezing.

questions.question: Salt is spread on roads in winter because it lowers the freezing point of water.
questions.explanation: Salt lowers water's freezing point, which helps stop ice from forming on roads.

questions.question: Why can water crack roads in winter?
questions.explanation: Water expands as it freezes and takes up more space, which can crack roads.

questions.question: Removing heat causes the particles in matter to ____.
questions.explanation: Taking heat away makes particles slow down, which can change a gas into a liquid or solid.

questions.question: Heating gives energy to particles and can change a solid into a liquid.
questions.explanation: Adding heat energy can melt a solid into a liquid.

questions.question: Which of these is a REVERSIBLE change?
questions.explanation: Melted ice can be frozen back into ice, so it is reversible. The others make new substances and cannot be undone.

questions.question: Identify the IRREVERSIBLE change.
options: A crumpled paper smoothed flat again
A wood log burning into ash
questions.explanation: Burning wood into ash cannot be undone — it is irreversible. The others can be reversed.

questions.question: Melting chocolate and then cooling it back into solid is a reversible change.
questions.explanation: You get back the solid chocolate you started with, so it is reversible.

questions.question: Dissolving sugar in water is an irreversible change.
questions.explanation: It is reversible — if the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind. The sugar did not become a new substance.

questions.question: Which change CANNOT be undone?
questions.explanation: Burning wood makes ash and smoke, which cannot turn back into wood — it is irreversible.

questions.question: Select ALL the IRREVERSIBLE changes.
questions.explanation: Burning paper and cooking an egg make new substances that cannot change back. Melting ice and freezing water can be reversed.

questions.question: Select ALL the REVERSIBLE changes.
questions.explanation: Melting wax, freezing water and dissolving sugar can all be reversed. Burning wood cannot.

questions.question: Neha's chocolate melted and then hardened in the fridge. Why is this a reversible change?
options: She got back the solid chocolate she started with
It made a brand new substance
questions.explanation: A change is reversible when you can get back what you started with — here, solid chocolate.

questions.question: Once wood turns to ash, it can become wood again.
questions.explanation: Burning is irreversible — ash cannot turn back into wood.

questions.question: Baking a cake is an example of a(n) ____ change.
questions.explanation: Baking makes a new substance (cake) that cannot be turned back into batter — it is irreversible.

questions.question: Which is an irreversible change in the kitchen?
questions.explanation: Cooking an egg makes a new substance that cannot be un-cooked — it is irreversible.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE?
questions.explanation: Reversible changes can be undone (like melting/freezing). Irreversible changes (like burning) cannot.

questions.question: A solution forms when a solute ____ in a solvent.
questions.explanation: A solution is made when a solute dissolves in a solvent, like salt in water.

questions.question: In salt water, the salt is the ____.
questions.explanation: The solute is the substance that dissolves — here it is the salt.

questions.question: In salt water, the water is the ____.
questions.explanation: The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving — here it is the water.

questions.question: Water is called the 'universal solvent' because it ____.
questions.explanation: Water can dissolve so many substances that it is called the universal solvent.

questions.question: When sugar fully dissolves in water it forms a ____.
questions.explanation: Sugar (solute) dissolving in water (solvent) forms a solution.

questions.question: The solute is the substance that dissolves.
questions.explanation: The solute dissolves; the solvent is the liquid that dissolves it.

questions.question: In a sugar-water solution, sugar is the solvent.
questions.explanation: Sugar is the solute (it dissolves). Water is the solvent.

questions.question: Honey stirred evenly into water forms a ____ solution.
questions.explanation: When honey dissolves evenly, the mixture is the same throughout — a homogeneous solution.

questions.question: A fizzy drink hisses as dissolved gas escapes. In this drink, the gas is the ____.
questions.explanation: The gas is dissolved in the liquid, so it is the solute.

questions.question: In the fizzy flavoured water, what is the solution?
questions.explanation: The whole flavoured sweetened water (solvent + dissolved solutes) is the solution.

questions.question: Why is the dissolved gas in soda considered a solute?
options: Because it is dissolved in the solvent
questions.explanation: Anything dissolved in the solvent is a solute — including a dissolved gas.

questions.question: Salt dissolving in water makes a ____ solution.
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt makes the water taste salty.

questions.question: In a solution, the solute is evenly spread through the solvent.
questions.explanation: When something dissolves, it spreads evenly through the solvent to make a solution.

questions.question: Substances that dissolve completely in a liquid are called ____.
questions.explanation: Soluble substances dissolve completely, like sugar in water.

questions.question: Substances that do NOT dissolve in a liquid are called ____.
questions.explanation: Insoluble substances do not dissolve, like sand in water.

questions.question: Which of these is SOLUBLE in water?
questions.explanation: Sugar dissolves completely in water, so it is soluble.

questions.question: Which of these is INSOLUBLE in water?
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve in water — it settles at the bottom, so it is insoluble.

questions.question: Select ALL the SOLUBLE substances.
questions.explanation: Salt and sugar dissolve in water. Sand and chalk powder do not.

questions.question: Select ALL the INSOLUBLE substances.
questions.explanation: Sand and chalk powder do not dissolve in water. Salt and sugar do.

questions.question: Sand added to water will settle at the bottom because it is insoluble.
questions.explanation: Insoluble sand does not dissolve, so it sinks and settles at the bottom.

questions.question: Sugar 'disappears' in water but the water still tastes sweet. This shows sugar is ____.
questions.explanation: The sugar dissolves (soluble) and spreads through the water, making it sweet even though you cannot see it.

questions.question: Statement 1: Sand and chalk powder do not dissolve in water. Statement 2: They are insoluble substances. Are both statements true?
questions.explanation: Both are correct — sand and chalk powder do not dissolve, which is exactly what 'insoluble' means.

questions.question: Why is an ocean oil spill so hard to clean up?
options: Oil is insoluble, so it floats and spreads on the surface
Oil dissolves everywhere so it spreads
Oil turns into a gas immediately
questions.explanation: Oil is insoluble in water — it does not dissolve, so it floats and spreads, making it hard to remove.

questions.question: Liquids that mix completely with each other are called ____.
questions.explanation: Miscible liquids mix fully into one solution, like water and alcohol.

questions.question: Liquids that do NOT mix and form separate layers are called ____.
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids do not mix — they stay in separate layers, like oil and water.

questions.question: Oil and water are ____ because they form separate layers.
questions.explanation: Oil and water do not mix; they form layers, so they are immiscible.

questions.question: Water and alcohol mixing into one solution are ____ liquids.
questions.explanation: They combine into one uniform mixture, so they are miscible.

questions.question: Trisha stirs lemon juice into water and it mixes fully. Lemon juice and water are ____.
questions.explanation: They mix completely into lemonade, so they are miscible liquids.

questions.question: Trisha stirs oil into water and it floats without mixing. Oil and water are ____.
questions.explanation: The oil floats and stays separate, so oil and water are immiscible.

questions.question: No matter how much you stir, immiscible liquids stay in separate layers.
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids like oil and water never mix into one, however hard you stir.

questions.question: Which pair is IMMISCIBLE?
questions.explanation: Only oil and water do not mix. The others mix completely.

questions.question: Which pair is MISCIBLE?
questions.explanation: Water and alcohol mix completely into one solution, so they are miscible. (Sand and stone are solids, not liquids.)

questions.question: Which method uses a barrier to separate solids from a liquid?
questions.explanation: Filtration uses a barrier (like cloth or a strainer) that lets liquid through but holds back solids.

questions.question: Using a strainer to remove tea leaves from tea is ____.
questions.explanation: The strainer is a barrier that catches the leaves while the tea passes through — filtration.

questions.question: Salt is collected from seawater by ____.
questions.explanation: The Sun evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind — that is evaporation.

questions.question: During salt production, what makes the water disappear from the shallow pools?
options: The Sun's heat evaporates it into the air
Workers scoop it out with buckets
The salt absorbs all the water
questions.explanation: The Sun's heat evaporates the water, leaving the salt behind.

questions.question: Heavier particles settling at the bottom of a still liquid is called ____.
questions.explanation: Sedimentation lets heavier particles settle at the bottom over time.

questions.question: Carefully pouring the clear liquid off the settled solids is called ____.
questions.explanation: Decantation separates the clear liquid from settled solids by gently pouring it off.

questions.question: A student pours too fast while decanting muddy water. What most likely happens?
options: The settled dirt is disturbed and mixes back in, spoiling the separation
The new container separates it automatically
questions.explanation: Pouring too fast stirs up the settled dirt so it mixes back into the clear water.

questions.question: A coffee maker's filter works by ____.
options: letting liquid through but holding the grounds back
questions.explanation: The filter is a barrier: liquid coffee passes through while the grounds are caught — filtration.

questions.question: Mud settling at the bottom of a glass of still water is an example of ____.
questions.explanation: The heavier mud particles settle at the bottom — that is sedimentation.

questions.question: Arjun's tank water is full of sand and small stones. Which method should he use to clean it?
questions.explanation: Filtration through cloth or a strainer separates the sand and stones from the water.

questions.question: In filtration, the cloth is a barrier. The water can ____ while the sand is ____.
questions.explanation: Water passes through the tiny holes, while the bigger sand and stones get caught behind the barrier.

questions.question: Water that has just been filtered through cloth is always safe to drink straight away.
questions.explanation: Filtering removes solid dirt, but tiny germs can still pass through, so the water is not necessarily safe to drink.

questions.question: Why is freshly filtered water not always safe to drink?
options: Germs can still pass through the filter
questions.explanation: Filtration only removes solid particles; germs and other harmful things may remain, so it needs further purification.

questions.question: To get pure salt from salt water you would use ____, because the salt is dissolved.
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt cannot be filtered out; evaporating the water leaves the salt behind.

questions.question: After sedimentation, the clear liquid on top is removed by ____.
questions.explanation: Once solids settle, you gently pour off the clear liquid — that is decantation.

questions.question: Sedimentation happens when a liquid is left undisturbed so heavier particles settle.
questions.explanation: Leaving muddy water still lets the heavier particles sink to the bottom — sedimentation.

questions.question: Select ALL the methods of separation.
questions.explanation: Filtration, evaporation, sedimentation and decantation are all ways to separate mixtures.

questions.question: Water can exist as solid ice, liquid water, and gas (water vapour).
questions.explanation: Water is a great example of matter that can be found in all three states.

questions.question: The water in your glass might once have been part of a ____.
questions.explanation: In the water cycle, water moves around Earth, so it may once have been part of a cloud.

questions.question: The water cycle works because water can ____.
options: change states and move around Earth
questions.explanation: Water constantly changes state (solid, liquid, gas) and moves around Earth in the water cycle.

questions.question: Dew forming in the morning is water vapour turning into liquid. This is ____.
questions.explanation: Water vapour (gas) cooling into liquid droplets of dew is condensation.

questions.question: Water vapour is the ____ state of water.
questions.explanation: Water vapour is water in its gas state.

questions.question: Ice is the solid state of water.
questions.explanation: When water freezes it becomes ice, the solid state of water.

questions.question: In lemonade, which is the solvent?
questions.explanation: Water is the liquid that dissolves the sugar and lemon, so water is the solvent.

questions.question: Sugar dissolved in hot water can be reversed by ____.
options: evaporating the water to get the sugar back
questions.explanation: If the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind, so dissolving sugar is reversible.

questions.question: Select ALL the changes that involve ADDING heat.
questions.explanation: Melting, boiling and evaporation all need heat added. Freezing happens when heat is removed.

questions.question: Select ALL the changes that involve REMOVING heat.
questions.explanation: Freezing and condensation happen when heat is taken away. Melting and boiling need heat added.

questions.question: Rock, pencil and desk are all examples of ____.
questions.explanation: They all keep a fixed shape and volume, so they are solids.

questions.question: Which best describes how a gas fills a room?
options: It spreads out to fill all the space
It sinks only to the floor
questions.explanation: A gas spreads out to fill any container or space it is in.

questions.question: Air can be seen easily with your eyes.
questions.explanation: Air is a gas you can feel but not see — like the air from a fan.

questions.question: Compressed air can fill a tire because a gas can be ____ into a smaller space.
questions.explanation: Gases can be compressed, so lots of air is squeezed into a small tire.

questions.question: Frost on a window is a gas turning straight into a ____.
questions.explanation: Water vapour turns directly into solid frost — this is deposition.

questions.question: Dry ice is special because it changes from solid straight to ____.
questions.explanation: Dry ice sublimates — it goes from solid directly to gas without becoming liquid.

questions.question: Which change cools a gas into a liquid?
questions.explanation: Condensation cools a gas into a liquid, like vapour forming droplets on a cold glass.

questions.question: When steam turns into water droplets as it cools, this is ____.
questions.explanation: Cooling steam (gas) into water (liquid) is condensation.

questions.question: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of matter — it has mass and takes up space.

questions.question: Water is used in so much cooking and cleaning because it ____.
questions.explanation: As the universal solvent, water dissolves many substances, which makes it great for cooking and cleaning.

questions.question: Select ALL the pairs of liquids that are MISCIBLE (mix completely).
questions.explanation: Lemon juice, alcohol and vinegar all mix completely with water. Only oil and water stay separate (immiscible).

questions.question: Which word describes a solid changing directly into a gas?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas, like dry ice.

questions.question: Which pair are BOTH reversible changes?
options: Burning wood and cooking an egg
Baking a cake and rusting iron
questions.explanation: Melting and freezing can both be undone, so both are reversible. The other pairs contain irreversible changes.

questions.question: A solute can be a solid, a liquid, or even a gas dissolved in a solvent.
questions.explanation: Sugar (solid) and the fizzy gas in soda are both solutes — anything dissolved in the solvent is a solute.

questions.question: Which property do all forms of matter share?
options: They have mass and take up space
questions.explanation: Every form of matter — solid, liquid or gas — has mass and takes up space.

questions.question: A balloon feels heavier when filled with air than when empty. What does this show?
options: Air has mass, so it adds weight
Air has no mass at all
questions.explanation: Since air is matter and has mass, a balloon filled with air weighs slightly more than an empty one.

questions.question: A shadow has mass and takes up space, so it counts as matter.
questions.explanation: A shadow is just the absence of light — it has no mass and takes up no space, so it is not matter.

questions.question: Which state of matter can be poured but keeps the same volume?
questions.explanation: A liquid can be poured and takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same.

questions.question: Why can a gas be squeezed into a much smaller cylinder, like in a gas cooking cylinder?
options: Gas particles are spread far apart and can be pushed closer together
Gas turns into a liquid automatically when squeezed
Gas has a fixed volume that cannot change
questions.explanation: Gas particles are normally spread far apart, so they can be pushed much closer together (compressed) to fit into a small cylinder.

questions.question: Solids, liquids, and gases are the three states in which matter is commonly found.
questions.explanation: These are the three common states of matter that matter can exist in on Earth.

questions.question: A sponge appears to change shape when squeezed. Why is it still classified as a solid?
options: It keeps its shape when released and does not flow like a liquid
It has no fixed shape at all, like a gas
It is actually a liquid soaked into fibres
It changes its own volume permanently when squeezed
questions.explanation: Even though a sponge can be compressed by squeezing, it returns to its original shape and does not flow, so it is still a solid.

questions.question: Select ALL the substances that are gases at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and helium are all gases at room temperature. Iron is a solid.

questions.question: What is the process called when a solid turns into a liquid?
questions.explanation: Melting is when a solid changes into a liquid, usually by adding heat.

questions.question: What is the process called when a liquid turns into a solid?
questions.explanation: Freezing is when a liquid changes into a solid, usually by removing heat.

questions.question: Which change happens when water is heated until bubbles rise quickly to the surface?
questions.explanation: Boiling is the rapid change of a liquid into a gas, seen as bubbles rising quickly when water is heated strongly.

questions.question: Evaporation only happens when a liquid is boiling, not at any other time.
questions.explanation: Evaporation can happen slowly at any temperature, like a puddle drying up in the sun, not just when boiling.

questions.question: A wet towel left outside dries up over a few hours, even without boiling. Which process explains this?
options: Evaporation — liquid water slowly turns into water vapour
Freezing — the water turns to ice
Melting — the towel is turning to liquid
questions.explanation: The liquid water in the towel slowly evaporates into water vapour (gas) in the air, even without reaching boiling temperature.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of deposition — a gas changing directly into a solid?
options: Frost forming on a cold window
questions.explanation: Frost forms when water vapour (gas) in the air changes directly into ice (solid) on a cold surface — this is deposition.

questions.question: Adding heat to ice causes it to ____.
questions.explanation: Adding heat to ice raises its temperature until it melts into liquid water.

questions.question: Which best explains why water in a pot boils faster on a stronger flame?
options: More heat energy is being added to the water in the same amount of time
A stronger flame removes heat faster from the water
Boiling never depends on how much heat is added
Stronger flames only affect the pot, not the water
questions.explanation: A stronger flame delivers more heat energy to the water more quickly, raising its temperature to boiling point faster.

questions.question: Removing heat from water vapour can cause it to condense into liquid water.
questions.explanation: When heat is removed from water vapour, it cools down and condenses into liquid water droplets.

questions.question: Select ALL of these everyday events that involve heat being ADDED to matter.
options: Butter melting on a warm stove
Ice cream melting in the sun
Water freezing into ice cubes in a freezer
questions.explanation: Melting butter, boiling water, and melting ice cream all require heat being added. Freezing water into ice happens when heat is removed.

questions.question: Which of these changes can easily be reversed (undone)?
questions.explanation: Melting ice can be reversed by freezing the water again. Burning, baking, and frying create changes that cannot easily be undone.

questions.question: Why is rusting of iron considered an irreversible change?
options: Once iron turns to rust, it cannot easily be changed back into pure iron
Rust can always be turned back into shiny iron by simply washing it
Rusting happens instantly and then disappears
Rusting is exactly the same as melting
questions.explanation: Rusting is irreversible because once iron combines with oxygen and water to form rust, it cannot easily be changed back into its original pure form.

questions.question: Tearing a piece of paper into small pieces is an irreversible change.
questions.explanation: Once paper is torn, it cannot be put back together into its original whole form, making it an irreversible change.

questions.question: Which pair below are BOTH examples of irreversible changes?
options: Folding paper and bending a wire
questions.explanation: Burning wood and cooking rice both create new substances that cannot be changed back to the original — both irreversible.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that are REVERSIBLE changes.
questions.explanation: Melting chocolate, freezing juice, and dissolving salt can all be undone. Baking bread creates a new substance that cannot be reversed.

questions.question: What do we call the substance that gets dissolved in a solution, such as sugar in water?
questions.explanation: The substance that gets dissolved, like sugar, is called the solute.

questions.question: Which best describes why salt seems to 'disappear' when stirred into water?
options: The salt dissolves into tiny particles spread evenly through the water
The salt turns into gas and floats away
The salt actually stops existing entirely
The water absorbs the salt's colour only, not the salt itself
questions.explanation: When salt dissolves, it breaks into tiny particles that spread evenly through the water, making it appear to disappear, even though it is still present.

questions.question: In a solution, the solute is evenly spread throughout the solvent.
questions.explanation: A key feature of a true solution is that the dissolved solute is spread evenly throughout the solvent.

questions.question: Why is seawater considered a solution?
options: Salt and other minerals are dissolved evenly throughout the water
It contains only pure water with nothing dissolved in it
The salt floats visibly on top of the water
Seawater is actually a solid, not a liquid
questions.explanation: Seawater is a solution because salt and various minerals are dissolved evenly throughout the water.

questions.question: A substance that dissolves completely in a liquid is called ____.
questions.explanation: A substance that dissolves completely, like sugar in water, is called soluble.

questions.question: Which of these is INSOLUBLE in water?
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve in water and will settle at the bottom — it is insoluble. Sugar, salt and coffee powder are all soluble.

questions.question: Chalk powder stirred into water will dissolve completely, leaving no residue.
questions.explanation: Chalk powder does not dissolve in water — it stays as tiny suspended particles or settles at the bottom, making it insoluble.

questions.question: Select ALL the substances that are generally SOLUBLE in water.
questions.explanation: Table salt, sugar and baking soda all dissolve completely in water. Sand does not dissolve and is insoluble.

questions.question: Two liquids that mix completely and do not separate are called ____.
questions.explanation: Miscible liquids mix completely and evenly, like alcohol and water.

questions.question: Why do oil and water separate into two distinct layers when mixed and left standing?
options: They are immiscible, meaning they do not mix together evenly
They are miscible and always mix perfectly
Oil dissolves completely into the water molecules
Water evaporates instantly when mixed with oil
questions.explanation: Oil and water are immiscible — they do not mix evenly and instead separate into two distinct layers over time.

questions.question: Vinegar and water are miscible, meaning they mix completely with each other.
questions.explanation: Vinegar mixes completely and evenly with water, making the two liquids miscible.

questions.question: Which method uses a cloth or strainer to separate solid particles from a liquid?
questions.explanation: Filtration uses a cloth or strainer with tiny holes to let liquid pass through while trapping solid particles.

questions.question: Which method would best separate salt dissolved in water back into solid salt?
options: Evaporation, which leaves the salt behind once the water dries up
Filtration, which cannot catch dissolved particles
Freezing, which does not remove the dissolved salt
Decantation, which only removes the top clear liquid
questions.explanation: Since salt is dissolved and cannot be filtered out, evaporation is used — as the water evaporates, the solid salt is left behind.

questions.question: Decantation involves carefully pouring off the clear liquid while leaving the settled solid behind.
questions.explanation: Decantation is the careful pouring off of the clear liquid on top after solids have settled to the bottom.

questions.question: Priya wants to separate small stones from muddy water she collected for a science project. What is the best FIRST step?
options: Let it settle (sedimentation), then filter or decant the water
Add more mud to the water
questions.explanation: The best approach is to first let the mixture settle (sedimentation) so heavier particles sink, then filter or decant to fully separate the clean water.

questions.question: Select ALL of these methods that can be used to separate mixtures of matter.
questions.explanation: Filtration, sedimentation and evaporation are all separation methods. Melting is a change of state, not a separation method.

questions.question: Which state of water do we drink from a glass?
questions.explanation: The water we drink from a glass is in its liquid state.

questions.question: Which best explains why puddles disappear on a hot, sunny day?
options: The liquid water evaporates into water vapour in the air
The water freezes into invisible ice
The water sinks permanently into the ground and never returns
The puddle turns into a solid overnight
questions.explanation: On a hot, sunny day, the heat causes the liquid water in the puddle to evaporate into water vapour, which is why the puddle disappears.

questions.question: Clouds are made up of tiny water droplets or ice crystals formed from condensed water vapour.
questions.explanation: Clouds form when water vapour condenses into tiny water droplets or ice crystals high in the sky.

questions.question: What word describes a substance changing from one state of matter to another?
questions.explanation: A change of state describes matter changing between solid, liquid, and gas forms.

questions.question: What word describes the mixture formed when a solute is fully dissolved in a solvent?
questions.explanation: When a solute is fully dissolved in a solvent, the resulting evenly mixed liquid is called a solution.

questions.question: Which of these best describes sublimation?
options: A solid changing directly into a gas without becoming liquid first
A liquid changing directly into a solid
A gas changing directly into a liquid
A solid melting into a liquid
questions.explanation: Sublimation is when a solid changes directly into a gas, skipping the liquid state entirely, as with dry ice.

questions.question: Naphthalene balls (mothballs) slowly disappearing over time in a closed cupboard is an example of sublimation.
questions.explanation: Naphthalene balls sublimate — they change directly from a solid into a gas, which is why they slowly shrink and disappear over time.

questions.question: Which of these best describes why a football can be inflated with air?
options: Air, a gas, can be compressed and pumped into the ball's flexible shape
Air is a liquid that fills the ball completely
Air is a solid that is pushed into the ball
Footballs cannot actually hold any air
questions.explanation: Air is a gas that can be compressed and pumped into a football, filling its flexible shape and making it firm.

questions.question: A scientist has a mystery substance that has no fixed shape and no fixed volume, spreading to fill any container. Which state of matter is it?
questions.explanation: A substance with no fixed shape and no fixed volume that spreads to fill any container is a gas.

questions.question: Which of these is a REVERSIBLE change?
options: Bending a wire into a new shape
questions.explanation: Bending a wire can often be bent back to its original shape, making it a reversible change, unlike burning, baking, or frying which create new substances.
